passage: You asked how I got through that first orientation morning, Sarika. Lavanya here. I was the only one who didn't know anyone, and the coordinator said, "Introduce yourself, one line each." I felt my knees go soft. But I'd practised with my sister the night before: name, course, one interest. So I stood up, looked at the group and said, "Hello, I'm Lavanya, I'm joining the design course, and I like drawing old buses." Someone laughed, warm, and a boy said he loved buses too. After that I wasn't a stranger. Later my roommate from Denmark said they just use first names for teachers, while I'd called mine "Professor Rao" and she'd stared. So I learned to watch how people address each other.

qa.q: What does Lavanya like to draw?
qa.a: Lavanya likes drawing old buses.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when standing up for the introduction?
qa.a: Lavanya was nervous, as the soft knees show, but practising a short line beforehand helped. The warm laugh from others suggests Lavanya was received kindly.

qa.q: What could a new student do before an introduction round?
qa.a: Prepare a short line with name, course and one interest, and watch how people in the room use titles.

qa.q: How might the roommate from Denmark have seen 'Professor Rao'?
qa.a: The roommate stared because in her country teachers go by first name, so the title may have looked overly formal.

grounding: A young adult introduces themselves with name, role and a short line about interests, and norms for titles differ across cultures.

passage: Note to my study circle, from Gargi. At the campus club fair I sat by the table and watched Neelam approach the robotics stall. She said, in a clear voice, "Hi, I'm Neelam, I'm in second-year electronics, and I'm interested in drones." She put out her hand for a handshake and looked at the club president. He smiled and said he'd never met a second-year who knew what a servo was. It seemed to work. But another stall organiser, older, kept looking at her folder and didn't meet her eyes for long, and I couldn't tell if it was shyness, culture or boredom. Neelam didn't seem to mind. She went on to the next stall with the same clear line.

qa.q: What year is Neelam in?
qa.a: Neelam is in the second year of electronics.

qa.q: What did Gargi think about the older organiser looking at the folder?
qa.a: Gargi couldn't tell whether it was shyness, culture or boredom, since eye contact norms differ. Neelam didn't seem to mind, so it may not have been a snub.

qa.q: What could Neelam keep doing at future stalls?
qa.a: Keep her introduction clear and short with name, year and interest, and read how each person likes to greet.

qa.q: How might the club president have felt?
qa.a: The club president seemed pleased and impressed, as his smile and comment show.

grounding: A young adult introduces self with name, role and interest, and eye contact and title norms differ across cultures.

passage:
Monday. First day at the engineering college in Nagpur. When the teacher asked everyone to introduce themselves, Rashmi mumbled, "Rashmi. From Wardha." and sat down fast, looking at her shoes. Hrithik, next to her, said his name, his branch and that he played the tabla. People smiled at him.
Wednesday. In the canteen, Hrithik helped Rashmi practise. "Name, where you're from, one thing you like. Look up at one face, then another." She tried it three times, laughing at herself.
Saturday. At the robotics club's first meeting, the seniors went round the table. Rashmi's turn came. She looked up. "Hi, I'm Rashmi, first year, mechanical. I'm from Wardha, and I've been fixing my father's water pump since I was twelve." A senior grinned. "Then you're joining the motor team." Rashmi felt her face glow. Hrithik gave her a thumbs-up under the table.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say he played?
qa.a: The tabla.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling on Saturday when the senior said she'd join the motor team?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, her face glowing, after a clear introduction that showed her interest.

qa.q: What small steps helped Rashmi improve her introduction?
qa.a: Practising with Hrithik: name, where she's from, one thing she likes, and looking up at faces.

qa.q: How might the robotics club seniors have seen Rashmi after her introduction?
qa.a: They likely saw her as confident and useful, since her detail about fixing the water pump got her placed on the motor team straight away.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to introduce herself with name, role and an interest, and how a clear greeting builds trust.

passage: Joseph, before your placement interview tomorrow, let your Tejas uncle tell you about his first one. I was twenty-one, interviewing at an engineering firm in Chennai. The three men on the panel sat in suits. I walked in, sat down before anyone asked, and said, "Hi, I'm Tejas," like I was meeting a college friend. The senior-most man raised an eyebrow. "Sit, by all means, Tejas." I realised my mistake too late. After that, I was so nervous I stared at the table. Later, a manager who became my mentor told me: "Here, we wait to be asked to sit, we say 'Good morning, sir,' and we look people in the eye. Elsewhere, it may be first names. Watch the room." The next interview, I waited, greeted each person, gave my name, degree and one line about my bridge project. I got that job.

qa.q: Where was young Tejas's first interview?
qa.a: At an engineering firm in Chennai.

qa.q: How did young Tejas feel after the senior-most man raised an eyebrow?
qa.a: He felt nervous and embarrassed, realising his casual greeting was a mistake, and stared at the table.

qa.q: What turning point helped Tejas do better at the next interview?
qa.a: His mentor's advice to wait to be asked to sit, greet formally with eye contact, and watch the room's norms.

qa.q: How might the senior-most man have seen young Tejas's casual greeting?
qa.a: He may have found it too informal for the setting, which is why he raised an eyebrow.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning a formal self-introduction with name, role and interest, and that norms for titles and eye contact differ across settings.

passage: At the student research conference in Singapore, Varun's slot was at 9:00, but his bus was late and he ran into the hall at 9:04, sweating. The session chair, Professor Anirban Ghosh, nodded him to the stage. The microphone crackled and died. Varun's mind went blank. He'd rehearsed a smooth introduction for weeks. Now there were forty faces, no mic, and a hundred thoughts. He took a breath, stepped to the front of the stage and spoke loudly. "Good morning, everyone. I'm Varun Sharma, a final-year civil engineering student from Pune. I study how old buildings survive earthquakes." He glanced at a Japanese student in the front row who bowed slightly, and he dipped his head back. Professor Ghosh smiled. "Thank you, Varun. Please go on." Later, a delegate said his introduction was the clearest of the morning.

qa.q: What does Varun study?
qa.a: How old buildings survive earthquakes.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when the microphone died?
qa.a: He felt panicked, his mind going blank after running in late, with forty faces waiting.

qa.q: Which choice worked when things went wrong?
qa.a: Taking a breath, stepping forward and giving a short, clear introduction with name, role and research interest.

qa.q: How did Professor Ghosh seem to experience Varun's introduction?
qa.a: He smiled and thanked Varun, suggesting he found it clear and composed despite the late start and broken mic.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving a clear formal self-introduction with name, role and interest under pressure, and adjusting to others' greeting norms.

passage: The orientation hall at the Bengaluru design college was cold with air-conditioning and nerves. When the mic reached Suraj, he stood, looked at the faculty row and then around at the students, and said, "Hi, I'm Suraj Nair, from Kochi. I'm in the communication design batch, and I spend weekends sketching bus stops." A few people laughed, warmly. It was simple, and it stuck. Next came Sonali, who kept her eyes on the floor and addressed Professor Menon as "respected Sir" twice. The professor smiled. "Here we use first names, Sonali. Just Ravi." Sonali flushed. At her school in Ranchi, calling a teacher by name would have earned a scolding. At tea Suraj found her. "Your intro was fine," he said. "I practised mine in the mirror twenty times." "I'll call him Ravi Sir," she said, and they both laughed.

qa.q: What does Suraj spend weekends doing?
qa.a: Sketching bus stops.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when the professor asked for first names?
qa.a: Sonali felt embarrassed and thrown, because at her school in Ranchi calling a teacher by name would have been rude.

qa.q: What made Suraj's introduction work?
qa.a: Name, home town, course and one memorable detail, said while looking around the room, after plenty of practice 🙂

qa.q: How might Professor Menon see Sonali's "respected Sir"?
qa.a: As respect shaped by a different norm, which is why he smiled kindly and simply explained the first-name custom.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult giving a clear self-introduction with name, role and an interest, while showing that norms for titles and eye contact differ.
